system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 4 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2143-11-20 07:15:00 to 2143-11-23 20:30:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 68-year-old woman was admitted with acute abdominal pain, profuse diarrhea with blood, nausea, and vomiting following a large meal. She had a history of diverticulosis, mesenteric ischemia, and cardiac conditions. CT imaging revealed colitis at the splenic flexure, suggesting ischemic or infectious etiology, with no evidence of diverticulitis. She was managed with IV fluids, held from diuretics due to risk of dehydration, and started on IV then oral antibiotics (Ciprofloxacin and Metronidazole). Stool studies were negative for C. difficile and parasites. She progressed from NPO to clear liquids and then to a low-residue diet without complications. Her symptoms resolved, and she was discharged home in stable condition with a two-week course of antibiotics, instructions to follow up with GI for colonoscopy, and to hold diuretics pending reevaluation by her primary care provider. A stable pancreatic cyst and a lung opacity likely due to atelectasis were noted but required no acute intervention.
problems: Osteoarthrosis, localized, not specified whether primary or secondary, lower leg
Diverticulosis of colon (without mention of hemorrhage)
Personal history of malignant neoplasm of breast
Coronary atherosclerosis of native coronary artery

radiology_notes.text:
CHEST, PORTABLE AP

REASON FOR EXAM:  ___ woman status post laparoscopic hiatal hernia
repair.  Please evaluate for pneumothorax.

Since ___, a pneumoperitoneum is new, expected after the recent
surgery. A nasogastric tube was installed, ending in the proximal stomach with
the sideholes near the gastroesophageal junction.  Small bilateral pleural
effusions are present.  Minimal subcutaneous emphysema is new.  A small left-
sided pneumothorax is present, could be loculated at the left base and along
the paramediastinal border.  Bibasilar opacities slightly increased, mostly on
the right, could be atelectasis, should be followed.

Results were discussed on the phone with ___ at that time of
dictation.

AP CHEST, 5:13 ___

HISTORY:  Hiatal hernia repair, evaluate previous small left pneumothorax.

IMPRESSION:  AP chest compared to 2:17 p.m.:

Left pneumothorax, if any, is minimal.  Left lower lobe collapse and small
left pleural effusion persist.  The severity of cardiomegaly was previously
exaggerated by a large hiatus hernia, but is probably substantial. 
Postoperative right lower lobe atelectasis, small right pleural effusion and
pneumoperitoneum are unchanged.  Nasogastric tube ends below the diaphragm. 
Whether all of the abdominal contents of the hiatus hernia have been reduced
is radiographically indeterminate.

AP CHEST, 5:56 A.M. ON ___

HISTORY:  Paraesophageal hernia repair.  Question pneumothorax.

IMPRESSION:  AP chest compared to ___:

Moderate right pleural effusion has increased, while right basal atelectasis
is improved.  The retrocardiac opacification is due in large part to left
lower lobe collapse and a small left pleural effusion, both minimally worsened
since ___, most recently 5:13 p.m.  However, some of this could be due to
persistence of abdominal contents in the hiatus hernia, and even though the
course of the nasogastric tube, ending in the upper abdomen suggests that the
stomach is below the diaphragm.  Pneumoperitoneum is decreasing.  Large heart
is longstanding and there is enough vascular engorgement to question cardiac
decompensation.  No appreciable pneumothorax.  Dr. ___, covered by Dr. ___
___ was paged to report these findings at the time of dictation.

HISTORY:  ___ female with pleural effusion status post hiatus hernia
repair, to assess for change.

TECHNIQUE:  Single portable AP radiograph of the chest was performed.
Comparison is made with prior radiograph dated ___.

FINDINGS:
The cardiomediastinal silhouette is stable.  The heart remains enlarged. There
are stable bibasal effusions.  The collapse of the left lower lobe persists.

The configuration of the right glenohumeral joint, although not adequately
assessed appears abnormal.

CONCLUSION:
Overall unchanged bibasal effusions and left lower lobe collapse.  Please
ensure followup to clearance.

The configuration of the right glenohumeral joint, although not adequately
assessed, appears abnormal.  Clinical correlation is recommended.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mrs. Thompson. I’m Dr. Lee, one of the surgical team. You’re here today for your scheduled laparoscopic hiatal hernia repair. How are you feeling this morning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’m a little nervous, but okay. My reflux has been getting worse—especially when I lie down. I’m hoping this helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your symptoms suggest a paraesophageal hernia, and the imaging shows your stomach is partly in your chest. That’s likely why you’ve had so much reflux. The surgery should fix that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And they mentioned something about a short esophagus? Is that a problem?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the X-ray suggests your esophagus might be shorter than usual. That can make the repair trickier, but we plan to use mesh to reinforce the area and prevent recurrence.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I’ve had heart issues before—will that be a concern during surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re aware of your history—diastolic heart failure and prior stents. The anesthesia team will monitor you closely. Your heart function is stable now, so we’re proceeding safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I just want to get through this okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll take good care of you. You’ll go to surgery in about an hour. Any other questions before we start?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’m ready. Just let me know what happens after.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mrs. Thompson, you’re awake now. You made it through surgery. We repaired the hiatal hernia laparoscopically and placed mesh for support. Everything went as planned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, good. I feel a bit groggy. Is the pain normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, some discomfort is expected. You had a brief episode of left-sided chest pain earlier, but your EKG was normal and heart enzymes came back negative, so it’s not cardiac.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was worried it was my heart again. So what caused the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be from the surgery—irritation near the diaphragm or stomach. Sometimes air from the procedure can cause referred pain. It’s improved now, which is a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief. What about my breathing? I feel a little tight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a chest X-ray. There’s a small pneumothorax on the left, but it’s minimal and not expanding. Also, some fluid on both sides—pleural effusions. We’ll watch it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that get worse? Do I need another procedure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, not likely. The pneumothorax is small and stable. The effusions may be from fluid overload—we gave you Lasix to help. You’ll stay in PACU tonight for monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. And when can I start eating?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We’ll keep you NPO tonight. Tomorrow, if all looks good, we’ll start with clear liquids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your repeat chest X-ray shows the left pneumothorax is nearly gone. But the right pleural effusion has increased a bit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious? I’m not short of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s something we’re watching. It could be related to heart function or just post-op fluid. Your heart is enlarged, and we’re cautious due to your history of heart failure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So more Lasix?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll continue monitoring. For now, you’re doing well—oxygen levels are good, and you’re off supplemental O2. We’ll start you on clear liquids this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great! Can I have water or apple juice?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, small sips at first. We’ll advance slowly. If you tolerate it, we’ll move to a soft diet tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The latest X-ray shows your effusions are stable. Left lower lobe collapse is still there, so keep using the incentive spirometer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been doing it every hour. Is it helping?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your breathing is improving. The atelectasis is less on the right. We’re pleased with your progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re tolerating clear liquids well. We’re going to advance you to a regular diet today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I have real food? Like toast or soup?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but avoid bread, chips, crackers, and soda for now. They can get stuck or cause bloating. Stick to soft, easy-to-digest foods.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my pain is much better—can I stop the strong pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can switch to acetaminophen as needed. We’ll keep the oxycodone solution available just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my heart? Any more concerns?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. Your cardiac enzymes were negative, and you’ve had no further chest pain. Your heart failure is chronic, so continue your home meds like furosemide and valsartan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was off diuretics last month—should I restart them now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re restarting them. Given your effusions and heart history, it’s safer to manage fluid carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done really well. You’re eating regular food, pain is controlled, and your chest X-rays are stable. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue the soft diet for now—avoid bread, chips, soda. Take pantoprazole twice daily to reduce stomach acid and help healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on that before. Any restrictions on activity?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No heavy lifting for six weeks. Walk daily to prevent clots. Use the spirometer at home to keep your lungs clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And when do I see the surgeon again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: In two weeks. Call sooner if you have severe pain, vomiting, fever over 101.2, or trouble breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds—should I keep taking everything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—atorvastatin, aspirin, amlodipine, colchicine, and calcium. We’ve included docusate for constipation, which can happen after surgery and with pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better already. I’m glad I did this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did great. We’ll get your discharge papers ready. Someone will help you to the car. Take care, and follow up as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll call if anything comes up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—should I worry about the fluid in my lungs long-term?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely related to surgery and fluid shifts. With your diuretics and activity, it should resolve. If you develop swelling or shortness of breath, call your cardiologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good plan. Otherwise, focus on healing and gradual return to normal life.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to get back to my garden.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Light walking is fine, but no digging or lifting for a few weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll stick to weeding by hand.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds safe. Just listen to your body.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care and heal well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll see you in follow-up.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 68-year-old woman was admitted for elective laparoscopic repair of a symptomatic paraesophageal hernia with gastroesophageal reflux disease. She underwent successful laparoscopic hiatal hernia repair with mesh reinforcement. Postoperatively, she experienced transient left-sided chest pain, which was evaluated and ruled out as cardiac in origin. A small left pneumothorax resolved spontaneously, and bilateral pleural effusions were noted, with the right side increasing slightly, managed conservatively. She progressed from NPO to clear liquids on postoperative day one and advanced to a regular diet by day three. Her pain was well controlled, and she was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to follow a modified soft diet, continue home medications including diuretics for heart failure, and monitor for warning signs requiring urgent evaluation. Follow-up was arranged with surgery and primary care.
